extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, editors and proofreaders (particularly crime/thriller authors and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writers and editors on choosing, placing, and omitting dialogue (speech) tags and using action beats so dialogue remains clear, natural, and in the foreground. Covers when to use 'said' or alternative tags, avoiding showy or non-speech tags, punctuation and rhythm, pronoun use, and tag omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialogue tag can come before, between or after direct speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement affects pace and rhythm: tags placed between speech can moderate pace by forcing a pause and break up longer chunks. Examples provided: before ('Dave said, "That’s the last thing..."'), between ('"That," said Dave, "is the last thing..."'), after ('"That’s the last thing...," Dave said.'). Consider the pacing and rhythm when choosing placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag function: indicate speaker, remain mechanical/background
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary function of a dialogue tag is mechanical: to indicate which character is speaking and remain largely invisible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace 'said' because its invisibility helps keep reader focus on the story rather than the tag. Tags should not draw attention away from the dialogue; they are part of the mechanics of story and should 'let the dialogue take the spotlight.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-tag guideline: don't trump the dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: A good tag doesn’t trump the dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the tag is more visible than the speech, it signals the dialogue itself needs enriching. Example anti-pattern: '"The way he was dressed, the attack was inevitable," preached McCready.' Better: rewrite the dialogue to convey the preaching tone and use a simple 'said' tag: '"Oh, come on," McCready said. "You dress like that..."'

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-tag guideline: don't repeat what dialogue already tells
rubrics_metrics.description: A good tag doesn’t repeat what the dialogue’s already told the reader (avoid double-telling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tags that restate information obvious from the dialogue or punctuation (e.g., 'exclaimed' after an exclamation mark). Common but less showy verbs like 'asked' and 'replied' are acceptable in moderation, but showy tags that duplicate the speech's content are redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-tag guideline: don't impair natural speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A good tag doesn’t impair how natural the speech sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags should not make dialogue sound stilted or unnatural. If a tag or its placement makes speech feel forced, choose a simpler tag, action beat, or rewrite the line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'said' and avoid deliberate avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Said' often works best because readers mostly do not notice it; avoiding 'said' deliberately can draw unwanted attention to the tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to avoid 'said' as a reflex; overusing alternative tags risks the reader focusing on the avoidance rather than the story. However, avoid placing 'said' after every expression (overuse). Examples show monotonous repetition as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expressive speech tags when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a tag that conveys sound quality, mood, or tone (e.g., 'whispered', 'yelled', 'muttered', 'whined') is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech tags can communicate manner when helpful, but they are not the only way—consider action beats or adverbial phrases as alternatives. Some tags (e.g., 'hissed') are stylistic choices that may divide opinion among editors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid showy tags that double-tell (opined/commanded/threatened/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Showy speech tags such as 'opined', 'commanded', 'threatened' often repeat what the dialogue already makes clear and are therefore redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the content of the dialogue demonstrates that an opinion, command, or threat is being given, consider a simple 'said' tag or no tag. Examples: '"But it’s none of our business...," opined Jack.' Consider whether 'said' would be less invasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non-speech-based tags (smiled, gesticulated, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs that describe physical expressions or body language (smiled, gesticulated, winced, scowled, laughed, etc.) jar when used as dialogue tags and introduce inauthenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These verbs are fine for describing actions but unsuitable as tags. Alternatives: use the verb in an action beat ('She laughed. "Martin..."') or use an adverb after a simpler tag ('she said, laughing'). Examples show undesirable usages and preferred alternatives with punctuation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action beats as alternatives/complements to tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich action beats can complement or replace speech tags, set the scene, and let the reader infer tone and manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep action beats on the same line as the speaker they're related to. They allow readers to fill in gaps and can prevent reliance on showy tags. Example: instead of '"My back teeth are killing me," James moaned.' use: 'James pressed two fingers to his cheek and winced. "My back teeth are killing me."' Note punctuation: there is a full stop after 'winced' in the example; punctuation choices affect flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and action-beat formatting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation around action beats and mid-sentence beats affects rhythm and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate punctuation choices: action beats can be a separate sentence before dialogue (with a full stop) or embedded with spaced en dashes for mid-sentence beats ('"You" – she smiled – "are the best thing..."'). The author notes US style alternatives (double quotes and closed-up em dashes). Choose punctuation that matches your style and maintains clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pronouns vs proper nouns in tags for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the characters' genders (or identities) are known to the reader, you needn't repeat the speaker's name every time in a tag; third-person singular pronouns (he/she) are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity is the priority—mix pronouns and proper nouns and pepper text with action beats so readers can track speakers. Examples from Alexander McCall Smith demonstrate mixing names and pronouns effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting dialogue tags when readers can track speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: You can omit dialogue tags altogether if the reader can reliably keep track of who’s speaking, typically when there are no more than two characters in the exchange and exchanges are short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most writers do not omit tags for long stretches; introduce a reminder tag or action beat after a few back-and-forths to maintain clarity. Example: Peter Robinson omits most tags in a two-character scene but uses an action beat and a tag midway to keep the reader on track.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-edit checklist for dialogue tags
rubrics_metrics.description: During self-editing, check tags to ensure they perform their indicative function without taking the spotlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific checks: ensure tags indicate who’s speaking rather than drawing attention; position tags to moderate pace and rhythm; avoid non-speech-related tags as tags; support dialogue with action beats so 'said' can remain invisible. This is a compact summary of the article’s core recommendations.
